deck: CS3307A OOD::Week 2::Interfaces vs Parameters vs Concretes

fields.Front: When should you use an interface?
fields.Back: When the variation is behavioral (different algorithms); enables polymorphism and DIP; consumers couple to the abstraction; flexible, extensible, testable.

fields.Front: When should you use parameters instead of subclasses?
fields.Back: When the variation is only data (numbers, labels, configs); keep one class configured via constructor arguments or fields; avoids subclass explosion.

fields.Front: When is a plain concrete class (no abstraction) acceptable?
fields.Back: For tiny apps or one-off utilities; simplest approach, but consumers are tied to the concrete implementation and it is harder to extend or swap later.

fields.Front: State the rule of thumb for choosing between interface, parameter, and concrete.
fields.Back: Behavior → Interface; Data → Parameter; Toy/simple case → Concrete.

fields.Front: What is wrong with DebugLogger and ErrorLogger in case study 1?
fields.Back: Both print to console and differ only in the prefix string ([DEBUG] vs [ERROR]); that is just data, so separate subclasses are pointless.

fields.Front: What is the right way to handle the logger level variation while keeping ILogger?
fields.Back: One parameterized concrete: ConsoleLogger(std::string lvl) storing level, printing [level] msg; callers hold ILogger&.

fields.Text: `{{c1::explicit}} on a single-argument constructor such as ConsoleLogger(std::string lvl) prevents implicit conversion from std::string to ConsoleLogger`.
`level({{c1::std::move}}(lvl))` moves the by-value constructor parameter into the member instead of copying it.

fields.Front: What is the trade-off of case study 2 (a Logger class with no interface)?
fields.Back: Minimal and fine for tiny apps, but callers depend on a concrete type; a new logging behavior (e.g., file) would force refactoring callers.

fields.Front: What role does AuditService play in case study 3?
fields.Back: High-level consumer: holds ILogger& logger (injected via constructor, aggregation) and calls logger.log(msg) polymorphically in record().
Dependency Injection: supplying a class's dependencies from outside (e.g., through the constructor) rather than creating them inside.

fields.Text: Rule of thumb: behavioral variation → {{c1::interface}}; data-only variation → {{c2::parameter}}; toy/simple case → {{c3::concrete}}.
Lesson of case study 1: when variation is only data (e.g., label text), don't make {{c1::subclasses}}; keep the interface and use {{c2::one parameterized class}}.
Case study 3 summary: when behavior differs, use {{c1::interfaces + DI}} to couple to the abstraction and swap implementations freely.
